# Markov Jump Processes



## Introduction and Motivation

In the previous chapter, we studied a two-state Markov model for an individual's mortality, where the possible states are Alive and Dead.

The model describes the movement between these two states over continuous time:

- An individual starts in the Alive state.
- The individual may move from Alive to Dead at any time.
- Once the individual enters the Dead state, no further transition is possible.

This is a simple example of a **continuous-time Markov model**.

We now extend this framework to models with more than two states, where transitions between states can occur over continuous time.

## From the Two-State Model to a General Model

The two-state mortality model can be represented by a continuous-time stochastic process $\{X(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$, where

$$
X(t)\in S=\{\text{Alive},\text{Dead}\}.
$$

More generally, we consider a stochastic process $\{X(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ that takes values in a finite or countable state space $S$.

Such a process is called a **Markov jump process**.

The process moves between states at random times and remains in each state for a random period before making a transition to another state.

## The Markov Property

A Markov jump process satisfies the **Markov property**: the future behaviour of the process depends only on its current state, rather than its previous history.

For all states $i,j\in S$ and times $s,t\geq 0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr\bigl(X(s+t)=j\mid X(s)=i,\\
&\qquad\qquad X(u),\,0\leq u<s\bigr)\\
&=\Pr\bigl(X(s+t)=j\mid X(s)=i\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, given the current state at time $s$, knowledge of the process's previous states does not provide any further information about its future state.

## Examples of Markov Jump Processes

Markov jump processes arise in many actuarial and financial applications.

- **Mortality models:** An individual moves from Alive to Dead.
- **Credit rating models:** A company moves between different credit rating categories, possibly including Default.
- **Insurance models:** An insurance policy moves between different states, such as Active, Lapsed and Surrendered.
- **Queueing models:** The number of customers in a service system changes as customers arrive and depart.

A familiar example is the **Poisson process**, which was introduced in the Actuarial Statistics course. Its state represents the number of events that have occurred by time $t$.

## Time-Homogeneous Markov Jump Processes

In this chapter, we focus on **time-homogeneous Markov jump processes**.

A Markov jump process is time-homogeneous if its transition probabilities depend only on the length of the time interval, rather than on the time at which the process starts.

For all states $i,j\in S$ and times $s,t\geq 0$,

$$
\Pr\bigl(X(s+t)=j\mid X(s)=i\bigr)
=p_{ij}(t).
$$

Here, $p_{ij}(t)$ denotes the probability that the process moves from state $i$ to state $j$ over a time interval of length $t$.

In particular, the transition probability does not depend on the starting time $s$.

This assumption allows us to describe the transition behaviour of the process using the length of the time interval alone.

## Discrete-Time and Continuous-Time Markov Models

The Markov chains studied previously are defined in discrete time, so transitions are observed at fixed time points.

In a Markov jump process, transitions can occur at any time, rather than only at integer multiples of a fixed time unit. The continuous-time framework provides a more flexible way to model systems whose states can change at any time.


The two models can be compared as follows:

| Discrete-Time Markov Chain | Continuous-Time Markov Jump Process |
|:---|:---|
| Time is discrete. | Time is continuous. |
| Transitions occur at fixed time steps. | Transitions occur at random times. |
| Described by a transition probability matrix. | Described by transition probabilities over a time interval. |
| The number of transitions is determined by the number of time steps. | The number of transitions by time $t$ is random. |







## Notation for Transition Probabilities

For a general Markov jump process, the transition probability from state $i$ at time $s$ to state $j$ at time $t$ is denoted by

$$
p_{ij}(s,t)
=
\Pr(X(t)=j\mid X(s)=i),
\qquad s\leq t.
$$

In actuarial notation, the survival probability ${}_t p_x$ and the death probability ${}_t q_x$ are special cases of transition probabilities in the two-state mortality model.

In particular,

- ${}_t p_x$ is the probability of remaining in the Alive state for at least another $t$ years.
- ${}_t q_x$ is the probability of moving from Alive to Dead within the next $t$ years.

## Transition Probabilities in the Time-Homogeneous Model

For a time-homogeneous Markov jump process, the transition probability depends only on the length of the time interval, rather than on its starting time.

Hence,

$$
p_{ij}(s,t)=p_{ij}(t-s).
$$

We therefore use the simplified notation

$$
p_{ij}(t)
=
\Pr(X(t)=j\mid X(0)=i).
$$

Here, $p_{ij}(t)$ denotes the probability of being in state $j$ after an interval of length $t$, given that the process starts in state $i$.

## Notation for Transition Rates

The transition rate from state $i$ to state $j$ at time $s$ is denoted by

$$
\mu_{ij}(s).
$$

For a time-homogeneous Markov jump process, the transition rates are constant. We therefore write

$$
\mu_{ij}(s)=\mu_{ij}.
$$

In the two-state mortality model, the transition rate from Alive to Dead is the force of mortality, denoted by $\mu_x$.

The transition rate may also be denoted by $\sigma_{ij}$ in some actuarial contexts.







# The Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations

## The Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations

The transition probabilities satisfy the initial condition

$$
p_{ij}(0)=\delta_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=j,\\
0, & i\neq j.
\end{cases}
$$

They also satisfy the **Chapman–Kolmogorov equations**:

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}(s+t)
=
\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}(s)p_{kj}(t)
}
$$

The equation considers all possible intermediate states $k$ at time $s$.

- $p_{ik}(s)$ is the probability of moving from $i$ to $k$ in time $s$.
- $p_{kj}(t)$ is the probability of moving from $k$ to $j$ in the following time interval of length $t$.

The equation follows from the Markov property and the law of total probability.

## Interpreting the Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations

Suppose the process starts in state $i$ at time $0$. To be in state $j$ at time $s+t$, the process must be in some intermediate state $k$ at time $s$.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij}(s+t)
&=\sum_{k\in S}
\Pr(X(s)=k\mid X(0)=i)\\
&\qquad\quad\times
\Pr(X(s+t)=j\mid X(s)=k).
\end{aligned}
$$

By time homogeneity, the two probabilities are $p_{ik}(s)$ and $p_{kj}(t)$, respectively.

Hence,

$$
p_{ij}(s+t)
=
\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}(s)p_{kj}(t).
$$

## Example: The Poisson Process

Consider a homogeneous Poisson process $\{N(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ with rate $\lambda$, where $N(t)$ is the number of events occurring in $(0,t]$.

The state space is

$$
S=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

By the independent and stationary increments properties,

$$
N(s+t)-N(s)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t),
$$

independently of the process up to time $s$.

If the process is in state $i$ at time $s$, it can only move to a state $j\geq i$.


## Example: The Poisson Process


Thus, its transition probabilities are

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}(t)=
\begin{cases}
e^{-\lambda t}
\dfrac{(\lambda t)^{j-i}}{(j-i)!},
& j\geq i,\\[8pt]
0, & j<i.
\end{cases}
}
$$

## Verifying the Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations

For the Poisson process, the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations give

$$
p_{ij}(s+t)
=
\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}(s)p_{kj}(t).
$$

Since the process can only move to higher states, the sum reduces to

$$
p_{ij}(s+t)
=
\sum_{k=i}^{j}p_{ik}(s)p_{kj}(t),
\qquad j\geq i.
$$


## Verifying the Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations


Substituting the Poisson transition probabilities,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij}(s+t)
&=e^{-\lambda(s+t)}
\sum_{k=i}^{j}
\frac{(\lambda s)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!}
\frac{(\lambda t)^{j-k}}{(j-k)!}\\
&=e^{-\lambda(s+t)}
\frac{\{\lambda(s+t)\}^{j-i}}{(j-i)!}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is precisely the transition probability $p_{ij}(s+t)$.

# The Transition Probability Matrix

## The Transition Probability Matrix

The matrix whose $(i,j)$-th entry is $p_{ij}(t)$ is called the **transition probability matrix**:

$$
P(t)=\bigl(p_{ij}(t)\bigr)_{i,j\in S}.
$$

For every $t\geq 0$, it is a stochastic matrix:

$$
0\leq p_{ij}(t)\leq 1,
\qquad i,j\in S,
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\sum_{j\in S}p_{ij}(t)=1,
\qquad i\in S.
}
$$

The transition probability matrix describes the distribution of the process at a future time, conditional on its current state.

## Matrix Form of the Chapman–Kolmogorov Equations

The Chapman–Kolmogorov equations can be expressed in matrix form as

$$
\boxed{
P(s+t)=P(s)P(t).
}
$$

This is the **semigroup property** of the transition probability matrices.

In particular,

$$
P(0)=I,
$$

where $I$ is the identity matrix.

Thus, the transition probability matrices of a time-homogeneous Markov jump process form a semigroup under matrix multiplication.

## Determining Probabilities from the Transition Matrix

Let the initial distribution of the process be

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}
=
\bigl(\mu_i^{(0)}\bigr)_{i\in S},
\qquad
\mu_i^{(0)}=\Pr(X(0)=i).
$$

The probability distribution of the process at time $t$ is

$$
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\mu}(t)
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}P(t).
}
$$

In particular,

$$
\Pr(X(t)=j)
=
\sum_{i\in S}\mu_i^{(0)}p_{ij}(t).
$$

Therefore, the initial distribution and the transition probability matrix determine the distribution of the process at any future time.

## Joint Probabilities at Several Time Points

Consider time points

$$
0<t_1<t_2<\cdots<t_n.
$$

By the Markov property and time homogeneity,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(X(0)=i_0,X(t_1)=i_1,\ldots,X(t_n)=i_n)\\
&\quad=
\mu_{i_0}^{(0)}
p_{i_0i_1}(t_1)
p_{i_1i_2}(t_2-t_1)
\cdots
p_{i_{n-1}i_n}(t_n-t_{n-1}).
\end{aligned}
$$

If the initial state is not specified, sum over all possible initial states:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(X(t_1)=i_1,\ldots,X(t_n)=i_n)\\
&\quad=
\sum_{i\in S}
\mu_i^{(0)}
p_{ii_1}(t_1)
p_{i_1i_2}(t_2-t_1)
\cdots
p_{i_{n-1}i_n}(t_n-t_{n-1}).
\end{aligned}
$$

# Transition Rates and the Generator Matrix

## Transition Rates

Transition probabilities describe the process over a time interval. To study its behaviour over a very short time interval, we introduce **transition rates**, also known as transition intensities.

For $i\neq j$, the transition rate from state $i$ to state $j$ is denoted by $q_{ij}$.

Assuming the transition probabilities are right-differentiable at $t=0$, define

$$
\boxed{
q_{ij}
=
p'_{ij}(0)
=
\lim_{h\downarrow 0}
\frac{p_{ij}(h)}{h},
\qquad i\neq j.
}
$$

The rate $q_{ij}$ describes the instantaneous rate of transition from state $i$ to state $j$.

For example, in a two-state mortality model, the transition rate from Alive to Dead is the force of mortality under the corresponding time-homogeneous assumption.

## Small-Time Behaviour of Transition Probabilities

Using a first-order Taylor expansion around $t=0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij}(h)
&=p_{ij}(0)+p'_{ij}(0)h+o(h)\\
&=\delta_{ij}+q_{ij}h+o(h),
\qquad h\downarrow 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}(h)\approx
\begin{cases}
1+q_{ii}h, & i=j,\\
q_{ij}h, & i\neq j.
\end{cases}
}
$$

For $i\neq j$, the probability of being in state $j$ after a short interval of length $h$, given that the process starts in state $i$, is approximately $q_{ij}h$.

The probability of remaining in state $i$ over the interval is approximately $1+q_{ii}h$.

## Properties of Transition Rates

The transition rates satisfy two important properties.

**1. Non-negative off-diagonal entries**

For distinct states $i$ and $j$,

$$
\boxed{
q_{ij}\geq 0,\qquad i\neq j.
}
$$

## Properties of Transition Rates


**2. Each row sums to zero**

Since the transition probabilities satisfy

$$
\sum_{j\in S}p_{ij}(t)=1,
$$

differentiating at $t=0$ gives

$$
\boxed{
\sum_{j\in S}q_{ij}=0.
}
$$

It follows that the diagonal entries are determined by the off-diagonal entries:

$$
\boxed{
q_{ii}=-\sum_{\substack{j\in S\\j\neq i}}q_{ij}.
}
$$

Thus, the diagonal entry is non-positive and represents the negative of the total rate of leaving state $i$.

## The Generator Matrix

The matrix whose $(i,j)$-th entry is $q_{ij}$ is called the **transition rate matrix** or **generator matrix**:

$$
Q=(q_{ij})_{i,j\in S}.
$$

Its entries satisfy

$$
q_{ij}\geq 0,\qquad i\neq j,
$$

and

$$
q_{ii}=-\sum_{j\neq i}q_{ij}.
$$

## The Generator Matrix


Hence, every row of $Q$ sums to zero.

The generator matrix describes the instantaneous transition behaviour of the process.

For a finite state space, the transition probability matrix can be determined from the generator matrix through the matrix exponential:

$$
\boxed{
P(t)=e^{Qt}.
}
$$

This relationship will be developed further when we study Kolmogorov's differential equations.











## Worked Example: A Two-State Markov Jump Process

Consider a time-homogeneous Markov jump process with two states, State 1 and State 2. The transition rates from State 1 to State 2 and from State 2 to State 1 are $\lambda$ and $\mu$, respectively, where $\lambda,\mu>0$.

1. Draw the state transition diagram.
2. Write down the transition rate matrix $Q$.

## Solution: Transition Rate Matrix

The diagonal entries are the negatives of the total rates of leaving each state.

- From State 1, the total rate of leaving is $\lambda$, so $q_{11}=-\lambda$.
- From State 2, the total rate of leaving is $\mu$, so $q_{22}=-\mu$.

The off-diagonal entries are the transition rates shown in the diagram. Hence,

$$
\boxed{
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\lambda & \lambda\\
\mu & -\mu
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

Each row sums to zero, as required.

The Dead state is absorbing: once the process enters this state, it cannot leave.

## Solution: Transition Rate Matrix

Using the state ordering $(h,i,d)$, the off-diagonal entries are determined by the transition rates in the diagram.

The total rate of leaving each state is:

- Healthy: $\sigma+\mu$;
- Ill: $\rho+\nu$;
- Dead: $0$.

Therefore, the diagonal entries are the negatives of these total rates.

The transition rate matrix is

$$
\boxed{
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
-(\sigma+\mu) & \sigma & \mu\\
\rho & -(\rho+\nu) & \nu\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

Notice that every row sums to zero, and all off-diagonal entries are non-negative.








## Worked Example: Generator Matrix of a Poisson Process

Consider a homogeneous Poisson process $\{N(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ with rate $\lambda>0$, where $N(t)$ represents the number of events that have occurred by time $t$.

The process is a time-homogeneous Markov jump process with state space

$$
S=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

1. Draw the state transition diagram.
2. Write down the transition rate matrix $Q$.


## Solution: State Transition Diagram

In a Poisson process, each event increases the number of events by exactly one. Therefore, the only possible transition from state $i$ is to state $i+1$, at rate $\lambda$.

The transition diagram is

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  scale=0.8,
  transform shape,
  state/.style={
    draw,
    circle,
    minimum size=0.85cm,
    inner sep=1pt
  },
  transition/.style={->, >=stealth, thick}
]
\node[state] (S0) at (0,0) {$0$};
\node[state] (S1) at (2,0) {$1$};
\node[state] (S2) at (4,0) {$2$};
\node (dots1) at (5.5,0) {$\cdots$};
\node[state] (S3) at (7,0) {$n$};
\node[state] (S4) at (9,0) {$n+1$};
\node (dots2) at (10.5,0) {$\cdots$};

\draw[transition] (S0) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} (S1);
\draw[transition] (S1) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} (S2);
\draw[transition] (S2) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} (dots1);
\draw[transition] (dots1) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} (S3);
\draw[transition] (S3) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} (S4);
\draw[transition] (S4) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} (dots2);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

## Solution: Transition Rate Matrix

The state space is countably infinite, so the generator matrix $Q$ is an infinite matrix.

From every state $i$:

- The rate of moving to state $i+1$ is $\lambda$.
- The total rate of leaving state $i$ is $\lambda$.
- All other transition rates are zero.

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\lambda & \lambda & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots\\
0 & -\lambda & \lambda & 0 & 0 & \cdots\\
0 & 0 & -\lambda & \lambda & 0 & \cdots\\
0 & 0 & 0 & -\lambda & \lambda & \cdots\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$


## Solution: Transition Rate Matrix


Equivalently, the entries of $Q$ are

$$
q_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
-\lambda, & j=i,\\
\lambda, & j=i+1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Every row sums to zero, and all off-diagonal entries are non-negative.












# Kolmogorov's Differential Equations

## From Transition Rates to Transition Probabilities

The generator matrix $Q$ describes the instantaneous transition rates of a Markov jump process.

However, in many practical applications, we are interested in probabilities such as:

- The probability of being in a particular state after $t$ years;
- The probability of moving from one state to another over a specified period;
- The probability distribution of the process at a future time.

Kolmogorov's differential equations provide the mathematical link between the **transition rates** and the **transition probabilities**.

Given the generator matrix $Q$, these equations can be solved to obtain the transition probability matrix $P(t)$.

## Practical Importance of Kolmogorov's Equations

In practice, the generator matrix is often estimated from observed data.

The general procedure is:

1. Collect data on the transitions between states and the time spent in each state.
2. Estimate the transition rates and construct the generator matrix $Q$.
3. Use Kolmogorov's differential equations to determine the transition probability matrix $P(t)$.
4. Use $P(t)$ to calculate probabilities and make predictions about the future behaviour of the process.

Thus, Kolmogorov's equations provide the link between statistical estimation of transition rates and the calculation of transition probabilities.

## Kolmogorov's Forward Differential Equations

For a time-homogeneous Markov jump process, the forward differential equations are

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d}{dt}p_{ij}(t)
=
\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}(t)q_{kj},
\qquad i,j\in S.
}
$$

In matrix form,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d}{dt}P(t)=P(t)Q.
}
$$

The initial condition is

$$
P(0)=I,
$$

where $I$ is the identity matrix.


## Kolmogorov's Forward Differential Equations


The forward equations describe how the transition probabilities change over time, starting from a specified initial state.





## Assumptions Underlying the General Markov Model

Consider a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain $\{X(t),t\geq 0\}$ with state space $S$.

The model is based on the following assumptions.

1. **Markov assumption:** The future state depends on the current state, but not on the previous history of the process.

2. **Transition intensity:** For distinct states $i$ and $j$,
   $$
   \Pr(X(t+h)=j\mid X(t)=i)
   =\mu_{ij}h+o(h),
   $$
   where $\mu_{ij}$ is the constant transition intensity from state $i$ to state $j$.

3. **Single-transition assumption:** The probability of two or more transitions during a short interval of length $h$ is $o(h)$.

Here, $h\downarrow 0$ and $o(h)$ denotes a quantity whose ratio to $h$ tends to zero.



## Small-Time Transition Probabilities

The assumptions imply the following approximations for a small time interval $h$.

For distinct states $i$ and $j$,

$$
p_{ij}(h)=\mu_{ij}h+o(h).
$$

For the probability of remaining in state $i$,

$$
p_{ii}(h)
=1-\sum_{j\neq i}\mu_{ij}h+o(h).
$$

Thus, the probability of leaving state $i$ during a short interval is approximately

$$
\left(\sum_{j\neq i}\mu_{ij}\right)h.
$$

## Small-Time Transition Probabilities


The total rate of leaving state $i$ is

$$
\lambda_i=\sum_{j\neq i}\mu_{ij}=-q_{ii}.
$$

These approximations form the basis for deriving the Kolmogorov forward equations.



## Derivation of the Kolmogorov Forward Equations

We use the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation:

$$
p_{ij}(t+h)=\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}(t)p_{kj}(h).
$$

For a small interval $h$, the probability of being in state $j$ at time $t+h$ has two main contributions:

- The process is already in state $j$ at time $t$ and remains there during the interval.
- The process is in another state $k\neq j$ at time $t$ and moves to state $j$ during the interval.




Using the small-time approximations,

$$
p_{ij}(t+h)=p_{ij}(t)\left(1-\sum_{\ell\neq j}\mu_{j\ell}h\right)+\sum_{k\neq j}p_{ik}(t)\mu_{kj}h+o(h).
$$

## Derivation of the Kolmogorov Forward Equations


Subtracting $p_{ij}(t)$, dividing by $h$ and letting $h\downarrow 0$ gives

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}'(t)
=
\sum_{k\neq j}p_{ik}(t)\mu_{kj}
-
p_{ij}(t)\sum_{\ell\neq j}\mu_{j\ell}.
}
$$

This is the Kolmogorov forward equation expressed in terms of transition intensities.



## Interpretation of the Forward Equations

The forward equation can be interpreted in terms of probability flow into and out of state $j$.

$$
\frac{d}{dt}p_{ij}(t)
=
\underbrace{\sum_{k\neq j}p_{ik}(t)\mu_{kj}}_{\text{Probability flow into state }j}
-
\underbrace{p_{ij}(t)\sum_{\ell\neq j}\mu_{j\ell}}_{\text{Probability flow out of state }j}.
$$

- **Inflow:** The process is in another state $k$ at time $t$ and moves to state $j$.
- **Outflow:** The process is in state $j$ at time $t$ and moves to another state.

The rate of change in the probability of occupying state $j$ is the total inflow minus the total outflow.

## Interpreting the Forward Equations

Consider the probability of being in state $j$ at time $t$, given that the process started in state $i$.

The forward equation is

$$
p_{ij}'(t)=\sum_{k\in S}p_{ik}(t)q_{kj}.
$$

The equation considers all possible states $k$ that the process may occupy at time $t$.

For each state $k$:

- $p_{ik}(t)$ is the probability of being in state $k$ at time $t$, starting from state $i$.
- $q_{kj}$ is the instantaneous transition rate from state $k$ to state $j$.

The forward equations therefore describe how probability flows into each destination state.

## Kolmogorov's Backward Differential Equations

The transition probabilities also satisfy the **backward differential equations**:

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d}{dt}p_{ij}(t)
=
\sum_{k\in S}q_{ik}p_{kj}(t),
\qquad i,j\in S.
}
$$

In matrix form,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d}{dt}P(t)=QP(t).
}
$$

The initial condition is again $P(0)=I.$


The backward equations describe how the transition probabilities change when we consider the possible first transitions from the initial state.

## Forward and Backward Equations: Comparison

Both equations describe the evolution of the same transition probability matrix, but they use the generator matrix in a different order.

| Forward equations | Backward equations |
|:--|:--|
| $P'(t)=P(t)Q$ | $P'(t)=QP(t)$ |
| Focus on the destination state | Focus on the initial state |
| Describe probability flow into destination states | Describe the effect of possible first transitions |


## Forward and Backward Equations: Comparison


For a finite-state, time-homogeneous Markov jump process, both equations lead to

$$
\boxed{
P(t)=e^{Qt}.
}
$$

Thus, either set of equations can be used to determine the transition probabilities.

The forward equations are often used to study the evolution of state probabilities, while the backward equations are useful in problems involving expected costs, rewards and times to reach specified states.

## Worked Example: A Two-State Markov Jump Process

Consider a time-homogeneous Markov jump process with two states, State 0 and State 1. For example, these may represent a healthy individual and a sick individual, respectively.

The transition rates are:

- $\lambda$ from State 0 to State 1;
- $\mu$ from State 1 to State 0.

The generator matrix is

$$
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\lambda & \lambda\\
\mu & -\mu
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \lambda,\mu>0.
$$


## Worked Example: A Two-State Markov Jump Process

**Questions**
1. Draw the state transition diagram.
2. Write down the forward differential equations.
3. Verify that the following expressions satisfy the forward differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{00}(t)
&=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}
+\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t},\\
p_{01}(t)
&=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}.
\end{aligned}
$$

4. Obtain expressions for $p_{10}(t)$ and $p_{11}(t)$.
5. Find the limiting transition probability matrix as $t\to\infty$ and interpret the result.


## Solution: State Transition Diagram and Forward Equations

The transition diagram is

```{=latex}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  scale=0.85,
  transform shape,
  state/.style={
    draw,
    rectangle,
    minimum width=2.2cm,
    minimum height=0.9cm,
    align=center
  },
  transition/.style={->, >=stealth, thick}
]
\node[state] (S0) {State 0};
\node[state, right=3cm of S0] (S1) {State 1};

\draw[transition]
  ([yshift=4pt]S0.east) -- node[above] {$\lambda$} ([yshift=4pt]S1.west);

\draw[transition]
  ([yshift=-4pt]S1.west) -- node[below] {$\mu$} ([yshift=-4pt]S0.east);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}


```

The forward equations are obtained from

$$
P'(t)=P(t)Q.
$$

For each initial state $i\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{i0}'(t)
&=-\lambda p_{i0}(t)+\mu p_{i1}(t),\\
p_{i1}'(t)
&=\lambda p_{i0}(t)-\mu p_{i1}(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

## Solution: State Transition Diagram and Forward Equations

The initial conditions are

$$
p_{ij}(0)=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=j,\\
0, & i\neq j.
\end{cases}
$$

## Solution: Transition Probabilities from State 0

Starting from State 0, the initial conditions are

$$
p_{00}(0)=1,
\qquad
p_{01}(0)=0.
$$

The forward equations become

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{00}'(t)
&=-\lambda p_{00}(t)+\mu p_{01}(t),\\
p_{01}'(t)
&=\lambda p_{00}(t)-\mu p_{01}(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the probabilities in each row sum to one,

$$
p_{00}(t)+p_{01}(t)=1.
$$

## Solution: Transition Probabilities from State 0


Substituting $p_{00}(t)=1-p_{01}(t)$ into the second equation gives

$$
p_{01}'(t)
=
\lambda-(\lambda+\mu)p_{01}(t).
$$

Solving this differential equation with $p_{01}(0)=0$ gives

$$
\boxed{
p_{01}(t)
=
\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
\left(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}\right).
}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
p_{00}(t)
=
\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}
+
\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}.
}
$$

## Solution: Transition Probabilities from State 1

Starting from State 1, the initial conditions are

$$
p_{10}(0)=0,
\qquad
p_{11}(0)=1.
$$

Using the forward equations and the condition

$$
p_{10}(t)+p_{11}(t)=1,
$$

we obtain

$$
p_{10}'(t)
=
\mu-(\lambda+\mu)p_{10}(t).
$$


## Solution: Transition Probabilities from State 1


Solving this differential equation gives

$$
\boxed{
p_{10}(t)
=
\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}
\left(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}\right).
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
p_{11}(t)
=
\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
+
\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}
e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}.
}
$$

## Solution: Transition Probability Matrix

Combining the four transition probabilities gives

$$
\boxed{
P(t)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac{\mu+\lambda e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}}
{\lambda+\mu}
&
\displaystyle
\frac{\lambda(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t})}
{\lambda+\mu}
\\[12pt]
\displaystyle
\frac{\mu(1-e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t})}
{\lambda+\mu}
&
\displaystyle
\frac{\lambda+\mu e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}}
{\lambda+\mu}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

Notice that each row sums to one, and $P(0)=I$.

## Solution: Limiting Transition Probability Matrix

As $t\to\infty$,

$$
e^{-(\lambda+\mu)t}\longrightarrow 0.
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to\infty}P(t)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}
&
\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
\\[8pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}
&
\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$


## Solution: Limiting Transition Probability Matrix


The limiting distribution is

$$
\boldsymbol{\pi}
=
\left(
\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu},
\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}
\right).
$$

Both rows of the limiting matrix are identical. Therefore, the limiting distribution does not depend on the initial state.

In the long run, the process spends a proportion $\mu/(\lambda+\mu)$ of its time in State 0 and a proportion $\lambda/(\lambda+\mu)$ of its time in State 1.

## Why the Backward Equations Are Useful

The forward equations describe how probabilities evolve from a given initial state.

The backward equations are useful when we want to study how the initial state affects a future quantity.

For example, let $g(j)$ be a cost or reward associated with being in state $j$ at time $t$. Define

$$
u_i(t)
=
\sum_{j\in S}p_{ij}(t)g(j).
$$

This is the expected cost or reward at time $t$, given that the process starts in state $i$.

Using the backward equations, we obtain

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d}{dt}u_i(t)
=
\sum_{k\in S}q_{ik}u_k(t).
}
$$

## Why the Backward Equations Are Useful


Thus, the backward equations can be used to study expected future costs and rewards from different initial states.

They are also useful in calculating expected times to reach a specified state, which we will consider later in this chapter.

## Interpretation of the Transition Probability $p_{ii}(t)$

It is important to distinguish between two different probabilities.

The transition probability

$$
p_{ii}(t)
=
\Pr(X(s+t)=i\mid X(s)=i)
$$

is the probability that the process is in state $i$ at time $s+t$, given that it was in state $i$ at time $s$.

It does **not** require the process to remain in state $i$ throughout the interval $[s,s+t]$. The process may leave state $i$ and return before time $s+t$.

In contrast, the probability of remaining continuously in state $i$ throughout the interval is

$$
\overline p_{ii}(t)
=
\Pr\bigl(X(u)=i\text{ for all }u\in[s,s+t]
\mid X(s)=i\bigr).
$$


## Interpretation of the Transition Probability $p_{ii}(t)$

For a time-homogeneous Markov jump process, this probability is

$$
\boxed{
\overline p_{ii}(t)=e^{-(-q_{ii})t}.
}
$$

Here, $-q_{ii}$ is the total rate of leaving state $i$.

In the two-state model, for example,

$$
\overline p_{00}(t)=e^{-\lambda t},
\qquad
\overline p_{11}(t)=e^{-\mu t}.
$$

These are the survival probabilities of the holding times in States 0 and 1, respectively.









## Worked Example: A Terminal Illness Model

Consider a three-state Markov jump process representing the health status of an individual:

- Well ($w$);
- Ill ($i$);
- Dead ($d$).

The transition diagram is shown below. The transition rates are $\sigma$ from Well to Ill and $\mu$ from Ill to Dead. Assume that both rates are constant.

1. Explain why $p_{ww}(t)=\overline p_{ww}(t)$.
2. Explain why $p_{ii}(t)=\overline p_{ii}(t)$.



## Solution: Interpretation of Transition Probabilities

The transition diagram is

\draw [shift={(460.87,100.37)}, rotate=539.7] [fill=black] (8.93,-4.29) -- (0,0) -- (8.93,4.29) -- cycle;

Since a transition from Ill to Well is impossible, once the process leaves the Well state, it cannot return.

Therefore, being in the Well state at time $s+t$ is equivalent to having remained continuously in the Well state throughout the interval $[s,s+t]$.

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
p_{ww}(t)=\overline p_{ww}(t).
}
$$


## Solution: Interpretation of Transition Probabilities


Similarly, once the process leaves the Ill state, it moves to the absorbing Dead state and cannot return to Ill. Thus,

$$
\boxed{
p_{ii}(t)=\overline p_{ii}(t).
}
$$

## Worked Example: Working, Retiring and Dying

Consider a time-homogeneous three-state Markov jump model for an individual's working life. The possible states are:

- Working ($w$);
- Retired ($r$);
- Dead ($d$).

Assume that the transition rates are constant. An individual can move from Working to Retired at rate $\nu$, or from Working to Dead at rate $\mu$. Both Retired and Dead are absorbing states.


## Worked Example: Working, Retiring and Dying

Answer the following questions:

1. What can you say about $p_{ww}(t)$ and $\overline p_{ww}(t)$?
2. Write down the forward differential equations for $p_{wd}(t)$, $p_{wr}(t)$ and $p_{ww}(t)$.
3. Solve the forward differential equation for $p_{ww}(t)$.
4. Show that

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{wd}(t)
&=\frac{\mu}{\mu+\nu}
\left(1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\right),\\
p_{wr}(t)
&=\frac{\nu}{\mu+\nu}
\left(1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

5. Verify that

$$
p_{wd}(t)+p_{wr}(t)+p_{ww}(t)=1.
$$


## Solution: Transition Diagram and Interpretation

The transition diagram is

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\resizebox{0.65\textwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.75pt,y=0.75pt,yscale=-1,xscale=1]
\draw (201.57,60.47) -- (349.67,60.47) -- (349.67,141.67) -- (201.57,141.67) -- cycle;
\draw (241.92,153.4) -- (200.02,189.36);
\draw [shift={(198.5,190.67)}, rotate=319.36] [fill=black] (8.93,-4.29) -- (0,0) -- (8.93,4.29) -- cycle;
\draw (318.23,200.97) -- (466.33,200.97) -- (466.33,282.17) -- (318.23,282.17) -- cycle;
\draw (86.23,197.63) -- (234.33,197.63) -- (234.33,278.83) -- (86.23,278.83) -- cycle;
\draw (326.92,156.4) -- (367.94,189.41);
\draw [shift={(369.5,190.67)}, rotate=218.82] [fill=black] (8.93,-4.29) -- (0,0) -- (8.93,4.29) -- cycle;
\draw (275.62,101.07) node [align=left] {{\fontfamily{ptm}\selectfont Working: $w$}};
\draw (204.37,159.3) node {$\nu$};
\draw (160.28,238.23) node [align=left] {{\fontfamily{ptm}\selectfont Retired: $r$}};
\draw (392.28,241.57) node [align=left] {{\fontfamily{ptm}\selectfont Dead: $d$}};
\draw (369.03,159.63) node {$\mu$};
\end{tikzpicture}%
}
\end{center}
```


## Solution: Transition Diagram and Interpretation


Since returning to the Working state is impossible, the probability of being in the Working state at time $t$ is equal to the probability of remaining continuously in that state.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
p_{ww}(t)=\overline p_{ww}(t).
}
$$

## Solution: Forward Differential Equations

Using the state ordering $(w,r,d)$, the transition rate matrix is

$$
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
-(\nu+\mu) & \nu & \mu\\
0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The forward equations are obtained from

$$
P'(t)=P(t)Q.
$$

Starting from the Working state, the relevant equations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{ww}'(t)
&=-(\nu+\mu)p_{ww}(t),\\
p_{wr}'(t)
&=\nu p_{ww}(t),\\
p_{wd}'(t)
&=\mu p_{ww}(t).
\end{aligned}
$$


## Solution: Forward Differential Equations


The initial conditions are

$$
p_{ww}(0)=1,
\qquad
p_{wr}(0)=p_{wd}(0)=0.
$$

## Solution: Probability of Remaining Working

The differential equation for $p_{ww}(t)$ is

$$
p_{ww}'(t)=-(\nu+\mu)p_{ww}(t).
$$

Solving this equation with $p_{ww}(0)=1$ gives

$$
\boxed{
p_{ww}(t)=e^{-(\nu+\mu)t}.
}
$$

Since $p_{ww}(t)=\overline p_{ww}(t)$, this is also the probability of remaining continuously in the Working state throughout the interval.

## Solution: Probabilities of Retirement and Death

From the forward equation for $p_{wd}(t)$,

$$
p_{wd}'(t)=\mu e^{-(\nu+\mu)t}.
$$

Integrating from $0$ to $t$, and using $p_{wd}(0)=0$, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{wd}(t)
&=\int_0^t\mu e^{-(\nu+\mu)s}\,ds\\
&=\boxed{
\frac{\mu}{\mu+\nu}
\left(1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\right).
}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
p_{wr}'(t)=\nu e^{-(\nu+\mu)t}.
$$


## Solution: Probabilities of Retirement and Death


Integrating and using $p_{wr}(0)=0$ gives

$$
\boxed{
p_{wr}(t)
=
\frac{\nu}{\mu+\nu}
\left(1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\right).
}
$$

## Solution: Verification of the Total Probability

Adding the three transition probabilities gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
&p_{ww}(t)+p_{wr}(t)+p_{wd}(t)\\
&=e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\\
&\quad+\frac{\nu}{\mu+\nu}
\left(1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\right)\\
&\quad+\frac{\mu}{\mu+\nu}
\left(1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\right)\\
&=e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}
+1-e^{-(\mu+\nu)t}\\
&=\boxed{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is consistent with the fact that an individual starting in the Working state must be in exactly one of the three states at time $t$.

## Worked Example: Permanent Health Insurance (PHI) Model

Consider a three-state model for permanent health insurance (PHI). This type of insurance provides a regular income to an individual who becomes unable to work because of long-term illness or injury.

The possible states are:

- Healthy ($h$);
- Ill ($i$);
- Dead ($d$).

Assume that the transition diagram is the same as the health-sickness-death model, with constant transition rates $\sigma$, $\rho$, $\mu$ and $\nu$.

1. Write down the forward differential equations for $p_{hh}(t)$, $p_{hi}(t)$ and $p_{hd}(t)$.
2. The equations for $p_{hh}(t)$ and $p_{hi}(t)$ can be solved simultaneously. Let

$$
u(t)=p_{hi}(t),
\qquad
w(t)=p_{hh}(t).
$$

Show that $u(t)$ satisfies the second-order linear differential equation

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d^2u}{dt^2}
+(\sigma+\mu+\rho+\nu)\frac{du}{dt}
+(\sigma\nu+\mu\rho+\mu\nu)u=0.
}
$$


## Solution: Transition Diagram and Generator Matrix

We assume that the transition diagram is the same as the health-sickness-death model:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\resizebox{0.65\textwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.75pt,y=0.75pt,yscale=-1,xscale=1]
\draw (20.57,59.47) -- (168.67,59.47) -- (168.67,140.67) -- (20.57,140.67) -- cycle;
\draw (171.25,81.07) -- (238.2,80.71);
\draw [shift={(240.2,80.7)}, rotate=539.7] [fill=black] (8.93,-4.29) -- (0,0) -- (8.93,4.29) -- cycle;
\draw (170.57,120.9) -- (240.75,121.07);
\draw [shift={(168.57,120.9)}, rotate=0.13] [fill=black] (8.93,-4.29) -- (0,0) -- (8.93,4.29) -- cycle;
\draw (242.23,59.97) -- (390.33,59.97) -- (390.33,141.17) -- (242.23,141.17) -- cycle;

\draw (316.28,100.57) node [align=left] {{\fontfamily{ptm}\selectfont Ill: \textit{i}}};
\draw (207.28,244.57) node [align=left] {{\fontfamily{ptm}\selectfont Dead: \textit{d}}};

```

Using the state ordering $(h,i,d)$, the transition rate matrix is

$$
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
-(\sigma+\mu) & \sigma & \mu\\
\rho & -(\rho+\nu) & \nu\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

## Solution: Forward Differential Equations

The forward equations are obtained from

$$
P'(t)=P(t)Q.
$$

Starting from the Healthy state, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{hh}'(t)
&=-(\sigma+\mu)p_{hh}(t)
+\rho p_{hi}(t),\\
p_{hi}'(t)
&=\sigma p_{hh}(t)
-(\rho+\nu)p_{hi}(t),\\
p_{hd}'(t)
&=\mu p_{hh}(t)+\nu p_{hi}(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

The initial conditions are

$$
p_{hh}(0)=1,
\qquad
p_{hi}(0)=p_{hd}(0)=0.
$$

## Solution: Deriving the Second-Order Differential Equation

Let

$$
u(t)=p_{hi}(t),
\qquad
w(t)=p_{hh}(t).
$$

The first two forward equations become

$$
\begin{aligned}
w'(t)
&=-(\sigma+\mu)w(t)+\rho u(t),\\
u'(t)
&=\sigma w(t)-(\rho+\nu)u(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the second equation gives

$$
w(t)=\frac{1}{\sigma}
\left\{u'(t)+(\rho+\nu)u(t)\right\}.
$$

## Solution: Deriving the Second-Order Differential Equation

Differentiating the equation for $u(t)$ gives

$$
u''(t)=\sigma w'(t)-(\rho+\nu)u'(t).
$$

Substituting the expression for $w'(t)$,

$$
u''(t)
=
\sigma\left\{-(\sigma+\mu)w(t)+\rho u(t)\right\}
-(\rho+\nu)u'(t).
$$

Now substitute

$$
w(t)=\frac{u'(t)+(\rho+\nu)u(t)}{\sigma}.
$$

## Solution: Deriving the Second-Order Differential Equation

After collecting terms, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
u''(t)
&=-(\sigma+\mu)u'(t)\\
&\quad-(\sigma+\mu)(\rho+\nu)u(t)
+\sigma\rho u(t)\\
&\quad-(\rho+\nu)u'(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging gives

$$
\boxed{
u''(t)
+(\sigma+\mu+\rho+\nu)u'(t)
+(\sigma\nu+\mu\rho+\mu\nu)u(t)=0.
}
$$

The initial conditions for this second-order equation follow from the original forward equations:

$$
u(0)=0,
\qquad
u'(0)=\sigma.
$$














# Holding Times and Occupancy Probabilities

## Holding Times in a Markov Jump Process

A Poisson process moves from state $i$ to state $i+1$ at each event. In a general Markov jump process, however, the process can move from its current state to any other state connected to it by a possible transition.

The timing of these transitions has a feature in common with the Poisson process: **the holding time in a given state is exponentially distributed**.

However, unlike the Poisson process, the parameter of the exponential distribution generally depends on the current state.

Let $T_0$ denote the first holding time:

$$
T_0=\inf\{t>0:X(t)\neq X(0)\}.
$$

Thus, $T_0$ is the time until the process first leaves its initial state.



## Distribution of the First Holding Time

Suppose the process starts in state $i$. The total transition rate out of state $i$ is

$$
\lambda_i=\sum_{j\neq i}q_{ij}=-q_{ii}.
$$

**Theorem:** Conditional on $X(0)=i$, the first holding time $T_0$ has an exponential distribution with parameter $\lambda_i$.

In particular, $\boxed{\Pr(T_0>t\mid X(0)=i)=e^{-\lambda_i t}=e^{q_{ii}t},\qquad t\geq 0.}$

If $\lambda_i>0$, the corresponding density is

$$
f_{T_0\mid X(0)=i}(t)
=\lambda_i e^{-\lambda_i t},
\qquad t\geq 0.
$$

If $\lambda_i=0$, state $i$ is absorbing and the process never leaves it.



## Interpreting the Holding-Time Distribution

The parameter $\lambda_i$ is the **total rate of leaving state $i$**. It is obtained by adding the rates of all possible transitions out of that state.

The probability of remaining in state $i$ for at least $t$ time units is

$$
\boxed{
\overline p_{ii}(t)
=\Pr(T_0>t\mid X(0)=i)
=e^{-\lambda_i t}.
}
$$

**We use an overline to denote this special probability, writing it as $\overline{p}_{ii}(t)$. This is the probability that the process remains in state $i$ throughout the entire interval $[0,t]$**.

The expected holding time in state $i$ is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{E}[T_0\mid X(0)=i]
=\frac{1}{\lambda_i}
=\frac{1}{-q_{ii}}.
}
$$

A larger total transition rate means a shorter expected holding time.



## Holding Times and the Poisson Process

The holding time in state $i$ has the memoryless property of the exponential distribution.

For $s,t\geq 0$,

$$
\Pr(T_0>s+t\mid T_0>s,\ X(0)=i)
=
\Pr(T_0>t\mid X(0)=i).
$$

Thus, conditional on still being in state $i$, the remaining time until the next transition has the same exponential distribution as the original holding time.

This is similar to the inter-arrival times of a Poisson process. The difference is that the rate of leaving a state in a general Markov jump process depends on the state currently occupied.



## Continuous Occupancy and Transition Probabilities

Two probabilities concerning state $i$ must be distinguished.

**Continuous occupancy probability**

$$
\overline p_{ii}(t)
=
\Pr(X(s)=i\text{ for all }0\leq s\leq t\mid X(0)=i).
$$

This is the probability that the process remains in state $i$ throughout the entire interval $[0,t]$.

**Transition probability**

$$
p_{ii}(t)
=
\Pr(X(t)=i\mid X(0)=i).
$$

This is the probability that the process is in state $i$ at time $t$. The process may have left state $i$ and subsequently returned.

## Continuous Occupancy and Transition Probabilities


Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
\overline p_{ii}(t)\leq p_{ii}(t).
}
$$

Equality holds when the process cannot return to state $i$ after leaving it.

For example, this equality holds in a model where state $i$ can only lead to absorbing states.

# The Jump Chain

## From Holding Times to the Jump Chain

A Markov jump process describes two aspects of the evolution of a system:

- **Timing:** how long the process remains in its current state before the next transition.
- **Destination:** the state to which the process moves when a transition occurs.

Suppose the process is currently in state $i$. The total rate of leaving this state is

$$
\lambda_i=-q_{ii}=\sum_{j\neq i}q_{ij}.
$$

The holding time in state $i$ is exponentially distributed with parameter $\lambda_i$.

## From Holding Times to the Jump Chain


When the process leaves state $i$, it moves to state $j$ with probability

$$
\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i},\qquad j\neq i.
$$

The next result shows that, conditional on the current state, the holding time and the destination of the next transition are independent.



## Distribution of the Next State

**Theorem:** Given that a time-homogeneous Markov jump process is currently in state $i$, where $\lambda_i>0$, the probability that it moves to state $j$ when it leaves state $i$ is

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X(T_1)=j\mid X(0)=i)
=\frac{q_{ij}}{-q_{ii}},
\qquad j\neq i,
}
$$

where $T_1$ is the time of the first jump.

Furthermore, the destination of the next transition is independent of the first holding time, conditional on $X(0)=i$.

Thus, the first holding time determines **when** the next transition occurs, while the transition probabilities determine **where** the process moves.



## Independence of the Holding Time and the Destination

The independence result can be seen from the joint probability density.

For a small interval $dt$, the probability that the process remains in state $i$ until time $t$ and then moves to state $j$ is approximately

$$
\Pr(T_1\in[t,t+dt),\,X(T_1)=j\mid X(0)=i)
=
e^{-\lambda_i t}q_{ij}\,dt.
$$

Since

$$
e^{-\lambda_i t}q_{ij}
=
\underbrace{\lambda_i e^{-\lambda_i t}}_{\text{Holding-time density}}
\underbrace{\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i}}_{\text{Jump probability}},
$$

the joint density factors into the product of the holding-time density and the jump probability.

Therefore, conditional on the current state, the holding time and the destination of the next jump are independent.



## Definition of the Jump Chain

Consider a time-homogeneous Markov jump process $\{X(t),t\geq 0\}$.

Let

$$
T_0=0
$$

and, for $n\geq 1$, let $T_n$ denote the time of the $n$th jump, where a jump is a transition to a different state.

Define

$$
X_n^*=X(T_n),\qquad n\geq 0.
$$

## Definition of the Jump Chain


The sequence

$$
X_0^*,X_1^*,X_2^*,\ldots
$$

records the states visited by the process at successive jump times.

This sequence forms a discrete-time Markov chain, called the **jump chain** or **embedded Markov chain**.

Unlike the original continuous-time process, the jump chain records only the sequence of states visited and ignores the time spent in each state.



## Transition Matrix of the Jump Chain

Let $P^*=(p_{ij}^*)$ denote the transition matrix of the jump chain.

If $q_{ii}<0$, the probability of moving from state $i$ to a different state $j$ at the next jump is

$$
\boxed{
p_{ij}^*=\frac{q_{ij}}{-q_{ii}},
\qquad j\neq i,
}
$$

with $p_{ii}^*=0.$


If $q_{ii}=0$, state $i$ is absorbing. We define

$$
p_{ii}^*=1,
\qquad
p_{ij}^*=0,\quad j\neq i.
$$

Thus, every row of $P^*$ sums to one.

The jump chain describes the sequence of states visited by the continuous-time process.



## Relationship Between the Markov Jump Process and Its Jump Chain

The Markov jump process and its jump chain describe the same sequence of state changes, but in different ways.

| Markov jump process | Jump chain |
|---|---|
| Continuous-time process | Discrete-time Markov chain |
| Records the time spent in each state | Ignores the holding times |
| Uses transition rates $q_{ij}$ | Uses transition probabilities $p_{ij}^*$ |
| Describes when and where transitions occur | Describes only the sequence of states visited |

The jump chain is useful for questions concerning the order in which states are visited.

For example:

- What is the probability of reaching state D before state H?
- What is the probability of visiting a particular state before reaching an absorbing state?
- What is the probability of eventually reaching a specified state?

These questions can be answered using the theory of discrete-time Markov chains.

# Expected Time to Reach a Given State

## Expected Time to Reach a Target State

Suppose we are interested in the expected time required for a Markov jump process to reach a specified target state $k$.

For example, in an actuarial model, we may wish to calculate:

- the expected time until a policyholder dies;
- the expected time until a policyholder becomes terminally ill;
- the expected time until a company reaches default.

Let $m_i$ denote the expected time to reach state $k$, given that the process starts in state $i$.

By definition,

$$
m_k=0,
$$

since the process has already reached the target state when it starts in state $k$.



## Recursive Formula for Expected Hitting Times

Suppose the process starts in a state $i\neq k$, with total transition rate

$$
\lambda_i=-q_{ii}>0.
$$

The process first spends a holding time in state $i$, whose expected value is

$$
\frac{1}{\lambda_i}.
$$

It then moves to another state $j$ with probability

$$
p_{ij}^*=\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i}.
$$

If the process moves to state $j$, the expected additional time required to reach state $k$ is $m_j$.

## Recursive Formula for Expected Hitting Times

Using first-step analysis,

$$
m_i
=
\frac{1}{\lambda_i}
+
\sum_{j\neq i}p_{ij}^*m_j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
m_i
=
\frac{1}{\lambda_i}
+
\sum_{\substack{j\neq i\\j\neq k}}
\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i}m_j,
\qquad i\neq k.
}
$$

The target-state term is omitted because $m_k=0$.



## Interpreting the Recursive Formula

The expected time to reach state $k$ consists of two parts:

$$
\underbrace{m_i}_{\text{Expected time to reach }k}
=
\underbrace{\frac{1}{\lambda_i}}_{\text{Expected holding time in }i}
+
\underbrace{\sum_{j\neq i}p_{ij}^*m_j}_{\text{Expected remaining time after the next jump}}.
$$

The first term is the expected time spent in the current state.

The second term is the expected time remaining after the process leaves the current state, averaged over all possible destination states.

The recursive equations are solved simultaneously for all non-target states.

If the target state cannot be reached with probability one, the expected hitting time may be infinite. A non-target absorbing state, for example, gives an infinite expected time to reach $k$.



## Worked Example: Expected Future Lifetime in the HSTD Model

Return to the four-state Health–Sickness–Terminally Ill–Death model.

Suppose the target state is Death (D), and let

- $m_H$ denote the expected future lifetime of a healthy life;
- $m_S$ denote the expected future lifetime of a sick life;
- $m_T$ denote the expected future lifetime of a terminally ill life.

**Questions**

1. Write down the recursive equations for $m_H$, $m_S$ and $m_T$, using the expected holding times and transition probabilities of the associated jump chain.

2. Solve the resulting system of simultaneous equations to determine the expected future lifetime of an individual who is initially in state H.


## (Brief) Solution to Worked Example: Expected Future Lifetime in the HSTD Model

Since Death is the target state,

$$
m_D=0.
$$

For each non-absorbing state, apply the recursive formula:

$$
m_i
=
\frac{1}{\lambda_i}
+
\sum_{j\neq i}p_{ij}^*m_j.
$$


This gives a system of three simultaneous equations.

Solving the system gives the expected future lifetime of a healthy life, $m_H$.

**The numerical solution depends on the transition rates specified in the HSTD model.**





# Observing a Markov Jump Process at an Arbitrary Time

## Residual Holding Time

So far, we have considered the first holding time when the initial state $X(0)$ is given.

We can extend this idea by observing the process at an arbitrary time $s>0$ and considering the additional time until its next transition.

Suppose that $X(s)=i$. The **residual holding time** is defined as

$$
T_s=\inf\{t>0:X(s+t)\neq X(s)\}.
$$

For a time-homogeneous Markov jump process,

$$
\boxed{
T_s\mid X(s)=i\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i),
}
$$

where

$$
\lambda_i=\sum_{j\neq i}q_{ij}=-q_{ii}.
$$

## Residual Holding Time

Consequently,

$$
\Pr(T_s>t\mid X(s)=i)=e^{-\lambda_i t}.
$$

The remaining time in state $i$ has the same exponential distribution, regardless of how long the process has already spent in that state.

## Distribution of the Next State at an Arbitrary Observation Time

Suppose that the process is observed in state $i$ at time $s$, where $\lambda_i>0$.

The probability that the next transition is to state $j$ is

$$
\boxed{
\Pr(X(s+T_s)=j\mid X(s)=i)
=\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i},
\qquad j\neq i.
}
$$

Thus, the probability of moving to a particular state at the next jump does not depend on the observation time $s$.

Furthermore, conditional on $X(s)=i$, the destination of the next transition is independent of the residual holding time $T_s$.

## Connection with the Results at Time 0

The results obtained at time 0 extend directly to an arbitrary observation time $s>0$.

In particular, conditional on the current state being $i$:

- The first holding time and the residual holding time have the same exponential distribution:

  $$
  T_0\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i),
  \qquad
  T_s\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i).
  $$

- The probability of moving to state $j$ at the next jump is the same:

  $$
  \Pr(\text{next state}=j)
  =\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i},
  \qquad j\neq i.
  $$

- In both cases, the holding time and the destination of the next transition are conditionally independent.


## Connection with the Results at Time 0


Therefore, the same distributions describe **when** the next transition occurs and **where** the process moves, whether it is observed at time 0 or at a later time.

These results provide the basis for describing the sequence of states visited at successive jumps, which leads to the definition of the **jump chain**.
